### Electrophysiology

HEK293T cells transfected with Cav1.2-GFP, Cavβ3, Cavα2δ1, and empty vector control (pcDNA3) or DsRed-Kv2.1P404W plasmids in a 1:0.5:0.5:1 ratio were seeded to microscope cover glasses (Fisher Cat# 12-545-102) approximately 15 hr prior to recording to obtain single cells. Coexpression of Cav1.2 and Kv2.1P404W in HEK293T cells was apparently cytotoxic and thus necessitated seeding of cells at a higher density to obtain viable single cells as compared to control cells expressing Cav1.2 alone. HEK293T cells were patched in an external solution of modified Krebs-Ringer buffer (KRB) containing (in mM): 146 NaCl, 4.7 KCl, 2.5 CaCl2, 0.6 MgSO4, 1.6 NaHCO3, 0.15 NaH2PO4, 8 glucose, 20 HEPES, pH 7.4, approximately 330 mOsm. Transfected cells were identified by the presence of GFP and DsRed expression. ICa was recorded in transfected cells using the whole-cell voltage clamp patch configuration using fire-polished borosilicate pipettes that had resistances of 2–3 MΩ when filled with an internal solution containing (in mM): 125 Cs-methanesulfonate, 10 TEA-Cl, 1 MgCl2, 0.3 Na2-GTP, 13 phosphocreatine-(di)Tris, 5 Mg∙ATP, 5 EGTA, 10 HEPES, adjusted to pH 7.22 with CsOH, approximately 320 mOsm. Currents were sampled at 20 kHz and low-pass–filtered at 2 kHz using an Axopatch 200B amplifier, and acquired using pClamp 10.2 software (Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA). All experiments were performed at room temperature (22–25°C). Pipette capacitance was compensated using the amplifier, and capacitance and ohmic leak were subtracted online using a P/5 protocol. Current–voltage (I–V) relationships were obtained approximately three minutes after obtaining the whole-cell configuration by subjecting cells to a series of 300 ms depolarizing pulses from the holding potential of −70 mV to test potentials ranging from −60 to +100 mV in 10 mV increments. The voltage dependence of G/Gmax was obtained from the recorded currents by converting them to conductances (G) using the equation G = ICa/(test pulse potential – Erev(Ca)), plotting the normalized values (G/Gmax) versus the test potential, and fitting them to a Boltzmann function. Steady-state inactivation was measured by subjecting cells to a series of 2500 ms conditioning prepulses from the holding potential to potentials ranging from −60 to +100 mV, returning to the −70 mV holding potential for 5 ms, then measuring the peak current elicited by a 300 ms step to the −20 mV test potential. Data were analyzed and plotted using Prism software (Graphpad Software Inc, San Diego, CA). For experiments in which depolarization-induced increases in Ca2+-sensitive dye were measured, we included 0.2 mM Rhod-2 (AAT Bioquest Cat# 21068) in the patch pipette solution. Images were acquired at 10 Hz using a through-the-lens TIRF microscope built around an Olympus IX-70 inverted microscope equipped with an oil-immersion ApoN 60×/1.49 NA TIRF objective and an Andor iXON CCD camera using TILLvisION imaging software (TILL Photonics, FEI, Hillsboro, OR).

To measure gating and ionic tail currents, we first determined the reversal potential for ICa from the I–V relationship obtained using the I–V protocol described above. Gating currents were then measured by applying a series of depolarizing steps from the holding potential (−70 mV) to potentials ± 5 mV of the reversal potential in 1 mV increments. Currents were sampled at a frequency of 25 kHz and low-pass filtered at 2 kHz. We first obtained recordings in cells perfused with KRB alone, then obtained recordings from the same cell after it had been perfused for two minutes with KRB containing 1 μM nitrendipine (Alomone Cat# N-155). To isolate gating currents and Itail produced by Cav1.2, we subtracted currents measured in the presence of nitrendipine from those measured in KRB alone. The on-gating charge (Qon) was then obtained from these records by integrating the gating current within approximately 2 ms of a depolarizing step to the reversal potential, and maximal Itail amplitudes were measured upon repolarization to the holding potential.

Somatic whole-cell patch clamp recordings were acquired from WT and Kv2.1 KO mouse CHNs cultured on microscope cover glasses after 15–16 DIV. Pyramidal neurons were selected based upon their morphological characteristics (Benson et al., 1994). Patch pipettes were fashioned and filled with intracellular recording solution as described above. After establishing the whole-cell configuration in KRB, the bath solution was exchanged with an extracellular recording buffer containing (in mM): 135 NMDG, 30 TEA-Cl, 5 BaCl2, 8 glucose, 20 HEPES, adjusted to pH 7.4 with HCl. Series resistance was 9.9 ± 0.9 (WT) and 10.4 ± 0.9 (Kv2.1 KO) MΩ (p=0.694, Student’s t-test) (before compensation); cell capacitance was 52.9 ± 4.8 (WT) and 58.4 ± 4.0 (Kv2.1 KO) pF (p=0.789, Student’s t-test). Prior to recording, cell capacitance was canceled, and series resistance was partially (60–70%) compensated. Recordings of LTCC ionic and gating currents were then performed as described for HEK293T cells. We used 10 µM nimodipine to isolate the contribution of LTCCs to the measured currents.

For simultaneous measurement of the Vm and Ca2+ sparks, rat CHNs transfected with GCaMP3-Kv2.1 were recorded using the whole-cell perforated patch clamp configuration. CHNs were patched in KRB using pipettes filled with a solution containing (in mM): 135 K-gluconate, 15 KCl, 5 NaCl, 1 MgCl2, 0.1 EGTA, 10 HEPES, pH adjusted to 7.22 using KOH, and amphotericin B (Millipore Cat# 171375) dissolved in DMSO and added at a final concentration of approximately 50 µg/mL. Upon obtaining a GΩ seal, the amplifier was switched to the current clamp mode to record spontaneous fluctuations in the Vm. Measurement of the Vm (sampled at 25 kHz) and widefield image acquisition (acquired at 5 Hz) were triggered simultaneously using the same microscope described above.

### Sparklets

We recorded Cav1.2-mediated Ca2+ sparklets using the dual TIRF imaging/patch clamp system described above. HEK293T cells transfected with untagged mouse Cav1.2, pDsRed-monomer-C1 or DsRed-Kv2.1P404W, Cavβ3, Cavα2δ1, and rat PKCα (Navedo et al., 2006), which increases spontaneous sparklet activity, were loaded via the patch pipette with a solution containing (in mM): 0.2 Fluo-5F (Invitrogen Cat# F14221), 87 Cs-aspartate, 20 CsCl, 1 MgCl2, 5 Mg∙ATP, 10 HEPES, 10 EGTA, adjusted to pH 7.2 with CsOH. After obtaining a GΩ seal in KRB, the external solution was exchanged with a solution containing (in mM): 110 NaCl, 5 CsCl, 1 MgCl2, 10 glucose, 10 HEPES, 20 CaCl2, pH 7.4 with NaOH. Cells were maintained at a holding potential of −70 mV, and TIRF images were acquired using TILLvisION software. Sparklets were manually detected and analyzed using Fiji software. Sparklet activity was quantified by calculating the nPs of each site (Navedo et al., 2006).

Acceptance summary:

This study by Vierra and colleagues describes the novel observation that the Kv2.1 voltage-activated potassium channel forms clusters that interact functionally with L-type voltage-activated calcium channels on the plasma membrane and with ryanodine receptors, an intracellular calcium channel that mediates release of calcium from intracellular stores. The authors show that CaV1.2 clusters increase in size with expression of Kv2.1, and that this effect also occurs with a mutant channel in which potassium permeation has been abolished, but not with a mutant channel exhibiting diminished clustering of the Kv2.1 channel. They also find that co-expression of Kv2.1 and CaV1.2 modulates the activity of this calcium channel by increasing the amplitude of calcium currents and shifting opening of the channel to more negative membrane voltages, making it easier for the channel to open in response to membrane depolarization. The editors and reviewers agreed that this is rigorous, well-executed study that presents important and original findings concerning the interaction of different ion channels involved in electrical signaling within neurons. The authors use an impressive number of tools and experimental approaches, the data are all very high quality and the manuscript is well-written. The experimental results all support the main claims of the paper and the authors were responsive to issues raised in review and have done an excellent job of revising the manuscript.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Kv2.1 mediates spatial and functional coupling of L-type calcium channels and ryanodine receptors in neurons" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Kenton Swartz as the Reviewing Editor and Eve Marder as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

All reviewers found your study on the role of Kv2.1 in functional coupling of Cav1.2 and ryanodine receptors (RyR) to be very interesting. The key findings of the manuscript are that clusters of Kv2.1 dynamically associate Cav1.2 and RyR, these associations result in discrete calcium signaling events (calcium sparks), and that Kv2.1 enhances Cav1.2 open probability. Although the functional significance of these clusters and their regulation remains speculative, the manuscript represents an important advance in our understanding of subcellular neuronal signaling and will be great of interest to the broader scientific community. We ask that you revise your manuscript to address the issues raised by the reviewers, as outlined below. Although we normally compile requests as essential or minor, in this case it may be helpful to see the reviewers remarks in the context of their reviews, and all reviewers have been clear about what is required and what is optional.

Reviewer #1:

The authors investigated the role of Kv2.1 in functional coupling of Cav1.2 and ryanodine receptors (RyR) to endow neurons with somatodendritic subcompartments capable of localized calcium signaling using a combination of antibody labeling with super-resolution microscopy, proteomics, in vitro calcium imaging, and patch clamp electrophysiology. While a nonconducting role for Kv2.1 in maintaining endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane junctions (EPJs) has been documented, the phenomenon's relevance to cellular function has generally been unclear. The key findings of the manuscript are that clusters of Kv2.1 dynamically associate Cav1.2 and RyR, these associations result in discrete calcium signaling events (calcium sparks), and that Kv2.1 enhances Cav1.2 open probability. The results look pretty solid, particularly as they were replicated in primary neuronal cultures, heterologous expression systems, and demonstrated in both rats and mice. Furthermore, the findings shed light on previous reports of localized RyR-mediated calcium events in acute hippocampal slice preparations. Although in the end, the functional significance of these clusters and their regulation remains speculative, the manuscript represents an important advancement in the understanding of subcellular neuronal signaling and will be great of interest to the broader scientific community.

1) There are inconsistencies in the quantitative rigor throughout the paper. In particular the lack of quantitative rigor for the results presented in Figure 1 is concerning. The majority of the results presented are strictly qualitative which is peculiar given the authors are equipped to measure colocalization. They do report that spatial distributions of Kv2.1 and Cav1.2 are correlated but is unclear exactly how this was ascertained other than using the analyze particles function of FIJI. Throughout the associated text, the authors make comparative statements "increased labeling in", less intense immunoreactivity", "comparable to". These statements should be bolstered by simple, unbiased image quantification and statistics. Furthermore, it is unclear why these experiments did not include an assessment Cav1.2 and ryanodine receptor spatial association in the Kv2.1-KO animal that the authors have access to and use throughout the paper. Quantification of spatial association in WT cultures and cultures from Kv2.1-KO animals is an important and simple experiment. Figure 2 also suffers similarly. Plots of colocalization like Figure 2K seem anecdotal. The use of CV as a relevant metric is not rationalized.

2) I am disappointed that the authors chose to convey the results of a key experiment, glutamate induced dispersal of Kv2.1 clusters, as a table as opposed to a figure. This seemingly crucial experiment demonstrates the ability of Kv2.1 to dynamically regulate, rather than an epiphenomenon of Cav1.2 and RyR clustering, and so it is unclear why it is relegated to a table. A possible answer is that the results are of marginal significance. If so, perhaps those data should be removed.

3) In a related concern, it would be beneficial to the interpretation of the experiment if the authors induced dispersal of Kv2.1 clusters with an alternative, preferably more direct, mechanism such as application of a PKA inhibitor. Given the expression of multiple metabotropic glutamate receptors in cultured hippocampal neurons, and the potential of metabotropic effects of NMDA receptor activation, the glutamate stimulation may not solely be acting through phosphorylation of Kv2.1. Although not essential to publication, this result would enhance the paper a lot.

4) In the results presented in Figure 3, the authors note large, synchronized calcium spikes associated with spontaneous action potentials. While the authors are likely correct that these represent a large increase in cytoplasmic calcium through action potential-associated voltage-gated calcium channels, this could be easily tested with the application of TTX. Furthermore, a key conclusion of the paper, that Cav1.2 and RyR associations "generate Ca2+ release events independently of action potentials" would be best demonstrated if the calcium sparks indeed persist in the presence of TTX. This experiment would also shed light on whether a neuron's spiking activity can affect frequency or amplitude of calcium sparks.

5) As with some other figures, the data in Figure 3E-G are presented anecdotally. E.g., the inset of 3E shows that Ca signals did not correspond to spontaneous depolarizations, but these are merely single traces. Do you infer that the apparent absence of a voltage signal associated with the spark implies that the spark is not being driven by a spatiotemporally localized Ca influx through LTCCs?

6) Figure 4 the black red and blue trace overlap so much one cannot tell anything from the data. For example, the red traces seem to show that thapsigargin did nothing.

Reviewer #2:

This study by Vierra et al. describes the novel observation that Kv2.1 channel form clusters that interact functionally with L-type Ca channels and ryanodine receptors. The authors show that CaV1.2 clusters increase in size with expression of Kv2.1, and that this effect occurs using a non-conducting mutant but is abolished in a non-clustering Kv2.1 mutant. Interestingly, they also find that co-expression of Kv2.1 and CaV1.2 (in HEK cells) increases the amplitude of whole-cell L-type Ca currents and leads to a leftward shift in the voltage-dependence of activation. In agreement with this finding, recordings in cultured hippocampal neurons from Kv2.1 KO mice show lower amplitude L-type Ca currents.

This is rigorous, well-executed study that presents important and original findings. The authors use an impressive number of tools and experimental approaches including immunohistochemistry, super resolution and TIRF imaging, electrophysiology, and mass-spec based proteomics. The data are all very high quality and the manuscript is well-written. The experimental results all support the main claims of the paper and the conclusions are all convincing.

1) The results shown in Figure 2E (effect of Kv2.1 non-clustering and non-conducting on CaV1.2 clusters) are quantified in terms of coefficient of variation (CV), but the rationale for this is not clearly described. Please address this. In addition to CV, the authors should also consider providing analysis/quantification of the absolute cluster size for each mutant tested as shown in Figure 2B.

2) The functional measurements of calcium sparks in Figure 3 and 5 show somewhat conflicting results. Results in Figure 5 show a reduction in spark amplitude with the non-conducting mutant, suggesting that conductance is necessary for increased amplitude. In Figure 3, however, the non-conducting Kv2.1 (P404W) mutant has no effect on amplitude of sparks (in comparison to the conducting Kv2.1). Why is this the case? Please discuss.

3) GCaMP3 and Cal-590 differ in their affinity for Ca2+, which may influence the apparent amplitude and size of the Ca sparks. This point may be helpful in addressing Comment 2. Along those lines, the spatial spread of the Ca signal (FWHM) is provided for the GCaMP3 images while the Cal-590 results are only provided as normalized values.

4) Along those lines, does expression of the Kv2.1 and the Kv2.1P404W mutants differ? This is relevant to GCamP3 fusion protein experiments. Please quantify.

5) The example CaV1.2 traces shown in Figure 6A show significant inactivation in the presence of Kv2.1. Was this generally true? Please address.

Reviewer #3:

In this paper by Vierra et al. the role for the potassium channel KV2.1 in the clustering and function of both voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) and ryanodine receptors (RyR) is explored in cultured neurons, cell lines, and tissues. The authors find that KV channels promote clustering of VGCC and RyRs. Furthermore, through imaging and ephys the authors show that this functional interaction lowers the activation threshold for calcium channels, promotes local calcium transients, and has a role in modulating the overall calcium signals in these cells. This tripartite interaction is proposed to occur specifically at PM-ER junction sites. In general, I find this paper well done and thorough. The experiments support the author's conclusions and I think it is a generally useful set of data for the field of cellular neuro-biology. I have some specific recommendations and comments that would improve the manuscript.

1) The zoom in Figure 1 (and most of the imaging based figures with small structures) makes it very difficult to evaluate the local clustering of these channels. As this concept is a key idea in the work (e.g. that these three proteins colocalize and functionally interact), can the authors please show more zoomed-in images, more direct measurements (plots) of the fluorescent signals, and less "wide-field" general views?

Also, some standard consistent quantitative way to evaluate co-localization would be helpful throughout the work. Something similar to a Pearson correlation co-efficient or similar type of analysis in most of the co-localization work should be presented across all relevant datasets in the figures.

2) In Figure 1D the KV signal from SIM looks very odd. Is this PM resident ER? Does a general ER marker have this same localization pattern?

3) In Figure 2 are the surface images here just single molecule-level KV? Specifically, is the "spottiness" of the KV images due to low labeling efficiency, low expression, or in fact due to clustering? Again, the size of the images makes it very difficult for me to evaluate the co-localization and cluster size of these signals.

4) The data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing ER morphology at the PM is key. My primary question is how much of the KV and VGCC proteins are inside the ER and how much are exposed at the plasma membrane. Because the effects shown in this paper are due to channels on the plasma membrane surface, a clear separation of these two populations is really important to understand this work. In general, I would like to know how much are functional channels (PM localized channel) and how much are non-functional ER localized channels before they have reached the PM. The data in Figure 2F in many ways addresses this question, but I would like to see these data analyzed and presented in a much more robust way. For example, given the difference between Figure 2A and 2F in the calcium channel signal it appears that most of the clustered VGCC signal is in the ER and not at the surface.

5) A general cartoon model of this complex should be in the main text of the paper as a figure.

[Editors' note: further revisions were requested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Kv2.1 mediates spatial and functional coupling of L-type calcium channels and ryanodine receptors in mammalian neurons" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers and the evaluation has been overseen by Eve Marder as the Senior Editor, and Kenton Swartz as the Reviewing Editor.

The editors and reviewers think you have done an excellent job of revising the manuscript to address the comments of the reviewers. Two of the reviewers have additional suggestions concerning the Pearson CC analysis, and we ask that you address these remaining issues in revision.

Reviewer #1:

In this revision of Vierra et al. the authors have made an excellent effort to address reviewer concerns. A small specific concern is listed below.

Regarding the added Pearson CC: what is being tested here? Codistribution across the image, or colocalization of pixels? SIM images do not indicate a degree of colocalization expected based on the assertion in the crosslinking analysis of 12 A distances. In fact the SIM images do not clearly show superposition of RYR and Cav1.2, only RYR and nearby 1.3 clusters. Some comment here would help. The Materials and methods do not really discuss the statistical tests, unless I missed it.

Reviewer #3:

I am generally satisfied with the revisions to the paper that have been made. The paper is now improved. I still do have one outstanding issue that the authors might consider addressing.

1) The use of Pearson's correlation coefficient (PCC) analysis was added to only the first and last figure as far as I can tell. Why was this not used throughout the paper? That being said the PCC values, while different from controls, are very low (0.2). A positive control should be up around 0.7-1. Can the authors discuss these low values as they relate to the findings of the paper? This indicates that the vast majority of these channels in neurons are not co-clustered.

The most useful place for this analysis would be in Figure 3 and in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2. Here, the PCC value would appear to be larger than in neurons but I can't tell because only raw line scans are shown and not PCC plots across multiple cells as a comparison.

In summary, I am trying to understand how common this complex is in both neurons and cultured cells. Do only a subset of ER/PM junctions have these complexes? If so how many? Are these functionally unique or different in some way? This would be useful to understand for this and future work.

claims.claim: VAP isoforms VAPA and VAPB are enriched in Kv2.1 immunopurifications from mouse brain.
claims.source: Similar to our earlier findings, enriched in the control Kv2.1 IPs (and absent from the Kv2.1 KO brain IPs) were the VAP isoforms VAPA and VAPB (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1 showing proteomic data.

claims.claim: RyR isoforms RyR2 and RyR3, LTCC α subunits Cav1.2 and Cav1.3, and various Cavβ auxiliary subunits are among the 50 most abundant proteins specifically present in Kv2.1 immunopurifications from mouse brain.
claims.source: In addition, among the 50 most abundant proteins specifically present in Kv2.1 IPs (i.e., from WT and not Kv2.1 KO brain samples) were numerous proteins involved in Ca2+ signaling and/or previously reported to localize to neuronal EPJs. These included RyR isoforms RyR2 and RyR3, the LTCC α subunits Cav1.2 and Cav1.3, various Cavβ auxiliary subunits of LTCCs, as well as other proteins involved in Ca2+ signaling and homeostasis (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1 showing proteomic data.

claims.claim: Kv2.1 is in close spatial proximity to LTCCs and RyRs at EPJs in mouse brain neurons.
claims.source: Taken together with our imaging analyses, these findings indicate that Kv2.1 is in close spatial proximity to LTCCs and RyRs at EPJs in mouse brain neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from imaging and proteomic data.

claims.claim: Cav1.2 is the predominant LTCC α1 subunit in hippocampus.
claims.source: We note that while Cav1.2 is the predominant LTCC α1 subunit in hippocampus (Hell et al., 1993; Davare et al., 2001; Moosmang et al., 2005; Lacinova et al., 2008; Sinnegger-Brauns et al., 2009), where its localization on neuronal somata overlaps with Kv2.1, it was not as highly represented in these proteomic analyses as was Cav1.3, perhaps as these analyses were performed on whole brain samples.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: In the presence of Kv2.1, Cav1.2 co-assembles into significantly larger clusters that show greater colocalization with the ER than in the absence of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: However, in the presence of Kv2.1, the organization of Cav1.2 was dramatically altered, such that Cav1.2 now co-assembled with Kv2.1 into significantly larger clusters (1.05 ± 0.67 μm2) that showed greater colocalization with the ER (as indicated by the PCC of Cav1.2-GFP and BFP-Sec61β) than in the absence of Kv2.1 (Figure 3B,D–F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3B,D-F showing TIRF imaging and analysis.

claims.claim: Kv2.1-induced rearrangement of Cav1.2 is accompanied by an increased occurrence of larger Cav1.2 clusters and a reduced occurrence of smaller Cav1.2 clusters in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: The Kv2.1-induced rearrangement of Cav1.2 was accompanied by an increased occurrence of larger Cav1.2 clusters and a reduced occurrence of smaller Cav1.2 clusters, and a nearly linear relationship between the sizes of Cav1.2 and Kv2.1 clusters (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3F showing cluster size analysis.

claims.claim: Cell surface Cav1.2-HA co-clusters with Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Similar to cells expressing fluorescently tagged channels, we found that cell surface Cav1.2-HA also co-clustered with Kv2.1 (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3H showing cell surface immunolabeling.

claims.claim: Kv2.1 does not alter the steady-state partitioning of Cav1.2 between PM and intracellular pools in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: We also determined that cell surface Cav1.2-HA immunolabeling corresponded to approximately 70% of the total Cav1.2 visible in the TIRF field regardless of Kv2.1 coexpression (Figure 3I), suggesting that Kv2.1 did not alter the steady-state partitioning of Cav1.2 between PM and intracellular pools.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3I showing quantification of surface vs. total Cav1.2.

claims.claim: Cell surface Cav1.2-HA cluster size is larger in the presence of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Importantly, similar to results obtained evaluating total Cav1.2, cell surface Cav1.2-HA cluster size was also larger in the presence of Kv2.1, indicating recruitment of cell surface Cav1.2 into larger clusters induced by Kv2.1 (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3I showing cluster size analysis.

claims.claim: Coexpression with Kv1.5 does not impact the clustering of cell surface Cav1.2 channels as does coexpression with Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: We also found that coexpression with the related but distinct Kv1.5 channel did not impact the clustering of cell surface Cav1.2 channels as did coexpression with Kv2.1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing immunolabeling.

claims.claim: Cells coexpressing Kv2.1 have higher CV values for cell surface Cav1.2 than cells coexpressing Kv1.5.
claims.source: We found that cells coexpressing Kv2.1 had higher CV values for cell surface Cav1.2 than did cells coexpressing Kv1.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1D showing CV analysis.

claims.claim: Cell surface Kv2.1 labeling exhibits greater colocalization with cell surface Cav1.2 than does cell surface labeling for Kv1.5.
claims.source: Cell surface Kv2.1 labeling also exhibited greater colocalization with cell surface Cav1.2 than did cell surface labeling for Kv1.5 (as indicated by PCC values, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1E showing PCC analysis.

claims.claim: The impact of Kv2.1 expression on Cav1.2 clustering does not require Kv2.1 K+ conductance.
claims.source: We next established that the impact of Kv2.1 expression on Cav1.2 clustering did not require Kv2.1 K+ conductance, as coexpression of a K+-impermeable point mutant (Kv2.1P404W) (Lee et al., 2003; Kirmiz et al., 2018b) induced clustering of Cav1.2 comparable to WT Kv2.1 (Figure 3J–K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3J-K showing imaging and analysis, with citations to Lee et al., 2003 and Kirmiz et al., 2018b.

claims.claim: Coexpression with a Kv2.1 point mutant deficient in clustering (Kv2.1S586A) has no effect on Cav1.2 clustering.
claims.source: Conversely, coexpression with a Kv2.1 point mutant (Kv2.1S586A), deficient in clustering (Lim et al., 2000) and in inducing EPJ formation (Kirmiz et al., 2018a; Kirmiz et al., 2018b), had no effect on Cav1.2 clustering (Figure 3J–K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3J-K, with citations to Lim et al., 2000; Kirmiz et al., 2018a; Kirmiz et al., 2018b.

claims.claim: Kv2.2 channels recruit Cav1.2 into large clusters in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: We also found that Kv2.2 channels similarly recruited Cav1.2 into large clusters (Figure 3L).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3L showing TIRF imaging.

claims.claim: The localization of GFP-tagged Cav1.3 is altered upon coexpression with Kv2.1 or Kv2.2 in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: We also determined that the localization of GFP-tagged Cav1.3 was similarly altered upon coexpression with Kv2.1 or Kv2.2, implying a common mechanism for co-clustering of these two neuronal LTCCs with Kv2 channels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C showing imaging.

claims.claim: Kv2.1 coexpression does not alter the PM localization of the T-type Ca2+ channel Cav3.1.
claims.source: In contrast, Kv2.1 coexpression did not alter the PM localization of the T-type Ca2+ channel Cav3.1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-F showing imaging and analysis.

claims.claim: The Kv2.1-mediated spatial reorganization of LTCCs is specific and related to their association with Kv2.1.
claims.source: This observation suggests that the Kv2.1-mediated spatial reorganization of LTCCs is specific and related to their association with Kv2.1 suggested by our Kv2.1 IP experiments, a notion also supported by the absence of T-type Ca2+ channels in these IP experiments.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claims.claim: Clustered but not non-clustered Kv2 channels enhance LTCC clustering and increase their localization to EPJs as a nonconducting function.
claims.source: Together, these data demonstrate that clustered but not non-clustered Kv2 channels enhance LTCC clustering and increase their localization to EPJs as a nonconducting function.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claims.claim: GCaMP3-Kv2.1 and GCaMP3-Kv2.1P404W are comparably expressed in surface-localized clusters in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: When expressed in HEK293T cells, GCaMP3-Kv2.1WT and GCaMP3-Kv2.1P404W were comparably expressed in surface-localized clusters as reported by both GxTX-633 labeling and GCaMP3 fluorescence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing imaging and quantification.

claims.claim: GCaMP3-Kv2.1 reports global Ca2+ spikes in rat CHNs.
claims.source: In rat CHNs, GCaMP3-Kv2.1 exhibited clustered localization similar to other fluorescently tagged Kv2.1 isoforms (Figure 4A) and reported global Ca2+ spikes, as indicated by the synchronized increase in fluorescence across the PM at sites where the construct was clustered and also in regions with diffuse GCaMP3-Kv2.1 expression (Figure 4B, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4A-B and Video 1 showing imaging.

claims.claim: Rapid and stochastic Ca2+ signals occur at a subset of individual GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters within the soma of rat CHNs.
claims.source: In addition to synchronized Ca2+ spikes, we also observed rapid and stochastic Ca2+ signals occurring at a subset of individual GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters within the soma (Figure 4B–C, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B-C and Video 1 showing imaging.

claims.claim: Ca2+ signals detected by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 are confined to individual clusters such that the fluorescence of adjacent clusters remains stable.
claims.source: These Ca2+ signals were confined to individual clusters such that the fluorescence of adjacent GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters < 1 µm from the active clusters remained stable (Figure 4B, compare regions of interest 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B showing fluorescence traces.

claims.claim: Ca2+ signal amplitude, frequency, and width detected by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 are insensitive to the K+ conductance of the reporter.
claims.source: We found that Ca2+ signal amplitude, frequency, and width were insensitive to the K+ conductance of the GCaMP3-Kv2.1 reporter, as Ca2+ signals detected by a K+-impermeable variant of this construct (GCaMP3-Kv2.1P404W) showed no difference in any of these parameters relative to GCaMP3-Kv2.1 (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4D showing quantification.

claims.claim: Spontaneous action potentials are associated with Ca2+ spikes reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in rat CHNs.
claims.source: Spontaneous action potentials were associated with Ca2+ spikes, suggesting that these synchronized, large-amplitude Ca2+ transients reflected Ca2+ entry through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels as well as Ca2+ release through RyRs (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4E showing simultaneous imaging and electrophysiology.

claims.claim: Localized Ca2+ signals reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 display no clear relationship with action potentials or other spontaneous Vm fluctuations.
claims.source: However, unlike global Ca2+ spikes, the localized Ca2+ signals displayed no clear relationship with action potentials or other spontaneous Vm fluctuations, similar to previous observations of localized Ca2+ release events in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Berrout and Isokawa, 2009; Manita and Ross, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Berrout and Isokawa, 2009 and Manita and Ross, 2009.

claims.claim: Localized Ca2+ signals reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 can persist in the presence of TTX.
claims.source: We also found that the localized Ca2+ signals could persist in the presence of TTX (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and that in some neurons, spark frequency appeared to be elevated immediately following a global Ca2+ spike (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C showing imaging data.

claims.claim: Localized Ca2+ signals arise independently of large, uniform fluctuations in the Vm such as those that occur with action potentials.
claims.source: Together, these observations suggest that the localized Ca2+ signals arose independently of large, uniform fluctuations in the Vm such as those that occur with action potentials.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claims.claim: Spontaneous, localized Ca2+ release events occur in the somata of non-transfected CHNs loaded with Cal-590 AM.
claims.source: Using this approach, it was possible to detect spontaneous, localized Ca2+ release events in the soma that were qualitatively similar to those recorded with GCaMP3-Kv2.1 (Figure 4F–G, Video 2), although with faster kinetics in fluorescence intensity changes relative to GCaMP3-Kv2.1, likely reflecting differences in the Ca2+ binding properties of these probes.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4F-G and Video 2 showing imaging.

claims.claim: Localized Ca2+ signals in CHNs loaded with Cal-590 AM occur primarily within the soma at sites of colocalized Kv2.1 and RyR clusters.
claims.source: Post-hoc immunolabeling of these CHNs for Kv2.1, RyRs, and the neuron-specific cytoskeletal protein MAP2 indicated that the observed localized Ca2+ signals occurred primarily within the soma at sites of colocalized Kv2.1 and RyR clusters (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4F showing post-hoc immunolabeling.

claims.claim: Caffeine enhances the frequency of localized Ca2+ signals reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in CHNs.
claims.source: We found that caffeine, which sensitizes RyRs to cytosolic Ca2+, enhanced the frequency of localized Ca2+ signals (Figure 5A,B, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A-B and Video 3 showing imaging data.

claims.claim: Depletion of ER Ca2+ stores with thapsigargin eliminates local Ca2+ signals reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in CHNs.
claims.source: In contrast, depletion of ER Ca2+ stores with the sarco-/endo-plasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) inhibitor thapsigargin led to an elimination of local Ca2+ signals (Figure 5A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A-B showing imaging data.

claims.claim: The LTCC agonist Bay K8644 increases Ca2+ spark frequency reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in CHNs.
claims.source: The frequency of these Ca2+ sparks was enhanced by activation of LTCCs with Bay K8644 (Figure 5A,B,D, Videos 4 and 5), while they were rapidly inhibited by blockade of LTCCs with nimodipine (Figure 5A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A-B,D and Videos 4-5 showing imaging data.

claims.claim: The LTCC inhibitor nimodipine rapidly inhibits Ca2+ sparks reported by GCaMP3-Kv2.1 in CHNs.
claims.source: The frequency of these Ca2+ sparks was enhanced by activation of LTCCs with Bay K8644 (Figure 5A,B,D, Videos 4 and 5), while they were rapidly inhibited by blockade of LTCCs with nimodipine (Figure 5A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A-B showing imaging data.

claims.claim: The subset of GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters that colocalize with RyRs correspond to the clusters that produce localized Ca2+ signals.
claims.source: Using this approach, we determined that the subset of GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters that colocalized with RyRs corresponded to the clusters that produced localized Ca2+ signals, either spontaneously or in response to the pharmacological modulators caffeine (Figure 5C) and Bay K8644 (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C-D showing post-hoc immunolabeling.

claims.claim: Neuronal Ca2+ spark frequency but not amplitude correlates with RyR cluster size.
claims.source: Similar to previous observations in vascular smooth muscle (Pritchard et al., 2018) and cardiac muscle cells (Galice et al., 2018), we found that neuronal Ca2+ spark frequency but not amplitude correlated with RyR cluster size, and that application of the LTCC agonist Bay K8644 steepened this relationship (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5E showing correlation analysis, with citations to Pritchard et al., 2018 and Galice et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Application of Bay K8644 steepens the relationship between Ca2+ spark frequency and RyR cluster size.
claims.source: Similar to previous observations in vascular smooth muscle (Pritchard et al., 2018) and cardiac muscle cells (Galice et al., 2018), we found that neuronal Ca2+ spark frequency but not amplitude correlated with RyR cluster size, and that application of the LTCC agonist Bay K8644 steepened this relationship (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5E showing correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Kv2.1-associated EPJs are sites of spontaneous CICR events mediated by LTCCs and RyRs.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations demonstrate that Kv2.1-associated EPJs are sites of spontaneous CICR events mediated by LTCCs and RyRs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claims.claim: Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyR2 can spatially associate in HEK293T cells in the presence of auxiliary subunits.
claims.source: We found that in the presence of these auxiliary subunits, Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyR2 could spatially associate in HEK293T cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6A showing TIRF imaging.

claims.claim: Spontaneous Ca2+ release events occur in HEK293T cells expressing Cav1.2, RyR2, and auxiliary subunits.
claims.source: Although it was not possible to establish whether a cell expressed all transfected constructs, we observed spontaneous Ca2+ release events in a subset of cells (Figure 6B,E) that were not seen in untransfected HEK293T cells and focused our analysis on cells that exhibited this phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6B,E showing TIRF imaging.

claims.claim: Spontaneous Ca2+ release events in HEK293T cells expressing Cav1.2, RyR2, and auxiliary subunits are rapidly blocked by the RyR inhibitor tetracaine.
claims.source: These spontaneous Ca2+ release events were rapidly blocked by the RyR inhibitor tetracaine (Figure 6G, Video 6), suggesting that they reflected CICR mediated by RyRs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6G and Video 6 showing imaging data.

claims.claim: Expressing Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells results in enhanced spark frequency and amplitude.
claims.source: Expressing Kv2.1 in these cells resulted in enhanced spark frequency and amplitude (Figure 6C–D,F,J).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6C-D,F,J showing imaging and quantification.

claims.claim: Expression of Kv2.1 channels capable of clustered EPJ formation (Kv2.1WT and Kv2.1P404W) increases spark frequency in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Expression of Kv2.1 channels capable of clustered EPJ formation (i.e., Kv2.1WT and Kv2.1P404W) increased spark frequency, whereas non-clustering Kv2.1S586A did not (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6J showing quantification.

claims.claim: Non-clustering Kv2.1S586A does not increase spark frequency in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Expression of Kv2.1 channels capable of clustered EPJ formation (i.e., Kv2.1WT and Kv2.1P404W) increased spark frequency, whereas non-clustering Kv2.1S586A did not (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6J showing quantification.

claims.claim: Spark amplitude is enhanced by K+-conducting Kv2.1WT but not Kv2.1P404W in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that spark amplitude was enhanced by K+-conducting Kv2.1WT but not Kv2.1P404W (Figure 6J), suggesting that while Kv2.1-mediated clustering alone was sufficient to impact spark frequency, K+ conductance was required to impact the amplitude of reconstituted Ca2+ sparks in HEK293T cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6J showing quantification.

claims.claim: Kv2.1-mediated clustering promotes the functional coupling of Cav1.2 and RyRs.
claims.source: In conclusion, these observations indicate that Kv2.1-mediated clustering promotes the functional coupling of Cav1.2 and RyRs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claims.claim: Expression of Cav1.2 with Kv2.1P404W enhances peak ICa compared to cells expressing Cav1.2 alone in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Consistent with an influence of Cav1.2 spatial organization on its activity, we found that expression of Cav1.2 with Kv2.1P404W enhanced peak ICa as compared to cells expressing Cav1.2 alone (Figure 7A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7A-B showing electrophysiology data.

claims.claim: Currents produced by Cav1.2 activate at more negative voltages in the presence of Kv2.1P404W than those produced by Cav1.2 alone in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Analysis of the conductance-voltage (G-V) relationship also showed an influence of Kv2.1 on the Vm threshold for Cav1.2 opening, with currents produced by Cav1.2 activating at more negative voltages in the presence of Kv2.1P404W than those produced by Cav1.2 alone, with no effect on steady-state inactivation (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7C showing G-V analysis.

claims.claim: There is a greater reduction in the fraction of peak current remaining after 250 ms of depolarization (r250) in cells coexpressing Cav1.2 and Kv2.1P404W, suggesting elevated Ca2+-dependent inactivation (CDI).
claims.source: However, we did observe a greater reduction in the fraction of peak current remaining after 250 ms of depolarization (r250), (Figure 7D), suggesting elevated Ca2+-dependent inactivation (CDI) of Cav1.2 in the presence of Kv2.1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7D showing r250 analysis.

claims.claim: Cells coexpressing STAC1 with Cav1.2 and Kv2.1P404W exhibit an increase in whole-cell ICa and a hyperpolarized shift in Cav1.2 opening.
claims.source: Cells coexpressing STAC1 with Cav1.2 and Kv2.1P404W also exhibited an increase in whole-cell ICa and a hyperpolarized shift in Cav1.2 opening, similar to results obtained without STAC1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C showing electrophysiology data.

claims.claim: In the presence of STAC1, Cav1.2 r250 values are comparable between control cells and cells expressing Kv2.1.
claims.source: However, in the presence of STAC1, which substantially reduces CDI in Cav1.2 (Campiglio et al., 2018), Cav1.2 r250 values were comparable between control cells and cells expressing Kv2.1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1D showing r250 analysis, with citation to Campiglio et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Kv2.1P404W enhances Cav1.2-mediated Ca2+ influx measured by Rhod-2 fluorescence in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Measurement of Ca2+-induced fluorescence increases in cells loaded with the Ca2+-sensitive dye Rhod-2 via the patch pipette also revealed an enhancing effect of Kv2.1P404W on Cav1.2-mediated Ca2+ influx (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7E showing fluorescence measurements.

claims.claim: HEK293T cells expressing Cav1.2 and either Kv2.1WT or Kv2.1P404W display greater K+-depolarization induced Ca2+ influx than control cells.
claims.source: Similarly, HEK293T cells loaded with the Ca2+ dye Fluo-4 and expressing Cav1.2 and either Kv2.1WT or Kv2.1P404W displayed greater K+-depolarization induced Ca2+ influx than control cells (Figure 7F–G), further supporting that K+-conducting as well as -nonconducting isoforms of Kv2.1 augment Cav1.2 activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7F-G showing fluorescence measurements.

claims.claim: Nitrendipine-sensitive Qon values produced by Cav1.2 alone are comparable to those measured in the presence of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Nitrendipine-sensitive Qon values produced by Cav1.2 alone were comparable to those measured in the presence of Kv2.1, indicating that the increased ICa in cells coexpressing Kv2.1 was not associated with an increase in the number of PM Cav1.2 channels (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7I showing gating current analysis.

claims.claim: The nitrendipine-sensitive Itail is significantly greater in the presence of Kv2.1 in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: However, the nitrendipine-sensitive Itail was significantly greater in the presence of Kv2.1, demonstrating that the open probability and/or conductance of Cav1.2 was increased when coexpressed with Kv2.1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7I showing tail current analysis.

claims.claim: The Kv2.1-dependent increase in ICa apparently comes from enhanced Cav1.2 voltage sensor coupling to channel opening.
claims.source: As comparable Qon values (i.e., Cav1.2 voltage sensor movement) produced a larger Itail in the presence of Kv2.1, these data taken together with the altered G-V curve shown in Figure 7C suggest that the Kv2.1-dependent increase in ICa apparently came from enhanced Cav1.2 voltage sensor coupling to channel opening.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the electrophysiology data.

claims.claim: Cells coexpressing Cav1.2 and DsRed-Kv2.1P404W display significantly more sparklets than control cells expressing Cav1.2 alone at a holding potential of −70 mV.
claims.source: In contrast, control cells coexpressing Cav1.2 and DsRed-Kv2.1P404W displayed significantly more sparklets than control cells expressing Cav1.2 alone and a higher level of basal activity as measured by nPs, where n is the number of quantal levels of Cav1.2 opening and Ps is the probability of sparklet occurrence (Figure 8C–E,I,J,L, Video 8).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 8C-E,I,J,L and Video 8 showing sparklet imaging and analysis.

claims.claim: DsRed-Kv2.1P404W coexpression results in near-maximal activation of Cav1.2-mediated sparklets at −70 mV holding potential.
claims.source: Interestingly, Bay K8644 treatment did not result in any further enhancement in nPs in cells expressing DsRed-Kv2.1P404W (Figure 8J), suggesting that DsRed-Kv2.1P404W coexpression may result in near-maximal activation of Cav1.2-mediated sparklets at this hyperpolarized membrane potential.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 8J showing sparklet analysis.

claims.claim: The nearest-neighbor distance (NND) of individual sparklet sites is significantly reduced in the presence of Kv2.1.
claims.source: Many sparklets occurred near clusters of Kv2.1 channels, and we found that the nearest-neighbor distance (NND) of individual sparklet sites was significantly reduced in the presence of Kv2.1 (Figure 8K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 8K showing NND analysis.

claims.claim: Kv2.1 enhances the open probability of Cav1.2 channels and increases the proximity of spontaneously active Cav1.2 channels to each other.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that Kv2.1 enhanced the open probability of Cav1.2 channels and increased the proximity of spontaneously active Cav1.2 channels to each other.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the sparklet data.

claims.claim: Whole-cell Ba2+ currents (IBa) at +10 mV are larger in CHNs from WT mice than those measured in Kv2.1 KO CHNs.
claims.source: Similar to the impact of Kv2.1 on LTCCs in HEK293T cells, whole-cell Ba2+ currents (IBa) at +10 mV (Figure 9A), as well as LTCC tail currents (Figure 9B,C) were larger in CHNs from WT mice than those measured in Kv2.1 KO CHNs (Figure 9A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 9A-C showing electrophysiology data.

claims.claim: The reduced IBa observed in Kv2.1 KO CHNs is primarily due to a reduction in the nimodipine-sensitive component of the current.
claims.source: To isolate the LTCC component of IBa, we applied the LTCC gating inhibitor nimodipine (10 µM), and found that the reduced IBa observed in Kv2.1 KO CHNs (Figure 9A–C) was primarily due to a reduction in the nimodipine-sensitive component of the current (Figure 9A,B,E), with no apparent difference in the nimodipine-resistant current (Figure 9A,B,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 9A-E showing electrophysiology data.

results.result: Kv2.1 channels spatially associate with LTCCs (Cav1.2 and Cav1.3) and RyRs in cultured hippocampal neurons (CHNs). Immunolabeling and super-resolution imaging show that Kv2.1 clusters often encompass smaller Cav1.2 and Cav1.3 clusters, and these are colocalized with RyRs. Spatial correlation analysis (PCC) demonstrates greater correlation between Cav1.2 and Kv2.1 than between Cav1.2 and Kv4.2, and nearest-neighbor distance analysis confirms non-random spatial distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C28 provide converging evidence from multiple imaging modalities (confocal, super-resolution SIM) and quantitative spatial analyses (PCC, nearest-neighbor distance) demonstrating spatial association of Kv2.1, LTCCs, and RyRs in CHNs. The use of Kv4.2 as a negative control (C22, C24) strengthens the specificity of the findings. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons (C24, C27).

results.result: The spatial coupling of Cav1.2 and RyRs is dynamically regulated by neuronal activity in CHNs. Glutamate stimulation reduces Kv2.1 clustering and decreases Cav1.2-RyR colocalization, RyR cluster size, and increases distance between Cav1.2 clusters. Conversely, TTX treatment increases spatial coupling between Cav1.2 and RyRs and increases RyR cluster size.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 demonstrate bidirectional regulation of LTCC-RyR spatial coupling by neuronal activity, with glutamate and TTX producing opposite effects. This is supported by quantitative morphological analysis (Figure 1J-N). The findings are consistent with known effects of these treatments on Kv2.1 phosphorylation and clustering, providing mechanistic plausibility.

results.result: Kv2.1 and Cav1.2 colocalize in hippocampal neurons in brain sections from rats and mice. Immunolabeling shows Cav1.2 concentrated in CA1 neuron somata with increasing labeling in CA2/CA3 and greatest in dentate gyrus (DG) granule cells. High-magnification imaging confirms Kv2.1 clusters colocalize with Cav1.2 clusters in DG and CA1 pyramidal neurons, with spatial association of Cav1.2, Kv2.1, and RyRs comparable to that in CHNs. Kv2.2 also colocalizes with Cav1.2.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 extend the spatial association findings from cultured neurons to intact brain tissue in both rats and mice, demonstrating the physiological relevance of the observations. The regional distribution patterns are consistent with prior literature (citations provided). The inclusion of Kv2.2 data (C36) suggests a conserved mechanism across Kv2 family members.

results.result: Crosslinking-based proteomic analysis identifies LTCCs and RyRs in close spatial proximity to Kv2.1 in mouse brain. VAP isoforms VAPA and VAPB, RyR isoforms RyR2 and RyR3, LTCC α subunits Cav1.2 and Cav1.3, and various Cavβ auxiliary subunits are among the 50 most abundant proteins specifically present in Kv2.1 immunopurifications from WT but not Kv2.1 KO brain samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 provide independent biochemical evidence supporting the spatial proximity of Kv2.1, LTCCs, and RyRs using crosslinking and mass spectrometry. The use of Kv2.1 KO samples as a negative control (C37, C38) is appropriate and strengthens the specificity of the findings. The proteomic data complement the imaging results and identify additional potential interacting proteins. The note about Cav1.2 vs. Cav1.3 representation (C40) acknowledges a limitation of using whole brain samples.

results.result: Kv2.1 induces clustering of Cav1.2 at ER-PM junctions in HEK293T cells. Coexpression of Kv2.1 with Cav1.2 results in significantly larger Cav1.2 clusters (1.05 ± 0.67 μm² vs. 0.27 ± 0.24 μm² alone) with greater colocalization with ER markers. Cell surface immunolabeling confirms that Cav1.2 co-clusters with Kv2.1 at the plasma membrane, with increased cluster size but no change in the proportion of Cav1.2 at the cell surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 demonstrate that Kv2.1 can induce LTCC clustering in a heterologous system, supporting a direct or indirect interaction. The use of TIRF microscopy and cell surface immunolabeling provides strong evidence for PM localization. Quantitative analysis shows significant increases in cluster size and ER colocalization. The finding that Kv2.1 does not alter surface/total Cav1.2 ratio (C44) indicates the effect is on spatial organization rather than trafficking.

results.result: The effect of Kv2.1 on Cav1.2 clustering is specific to Kv2.1 and not shared by the related channel Kv1.5. Cells coexpressing Kv2.1 have higher CV values for cell surface Cav1.2 and greater colocalization (PCC) with Cav1.2 than cells coexpressing Kv1.5.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 provide important specificity controls demonstrating that the clustering effect is not a general property of voltage-gated K+ channels. The use of CV and PCC as quantitative measures strengthens the comparison. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons (C47, C48).

results.result: Kv2.1-induced clustering of LTCCs is independent of K+ conductance but requires Kv2.1's ability to cluster and form EPJs. The nonconducting Kv2.1P404W mutant induces Cav1.2 clustering comparable to WT Kv2.1, while the non-clustering Kv2.1S586A mutant has no effect. Kv2.2 similarly recruits Cav1.2 into large clusters. Cav1.3 localization is also altered by Kv2.1 or Kv2.2 coexpression, but Kv2.1 does not alter Cav3.1 (T-type Ca2+ channel) localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C55 use well-characterized Kv2.1 mutants to dissect the mechanism of LTCC clustering. The findings that clustering but not conductance is required (C49, C50) are supported by appropriate controls. The specificity for LTCCs (Cav1.2, Cav1.3) but not T-type channels (Cav3.1) (C53) is important for understanding the mechanism. The extension to Kv2.2 (C51) suggests a conserved function.

results.result: GCaMP3-Kv2.1 reports both global Ca2+ spikes and localized Ca2+ signals at individual Kv2.1 clusters in rat CHNs. The localized Ca2+ signals are confined to individual clusters, occur independently of action potentials, and are insensitive to the K+ conductance of the reporter. Spontaneous action potentials are associated with global Ca2+ spikes, but localized signals display no clear relationship with action potentials or Vm fluctuations and can persist in the presence of TTX.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C64 establish the use of GCaMP3-Kv2.1 as a reporter for Ca2+ signals at Kv2.1-associated EPJs. The findings that localized signals are independent of K+ conductance (C60) and action potentials (C62, C63) are well-supported by simultaneous imaging and electrophysiology (C61) and TTX experiments (C63). The spatial confinement of signals (C59) is important for establishing compartmentalization.

results.result: Spontaneous, localized Ca2+ release events occur in non-transfected CHNs loaded with Cal-590 AM, primarily within the soma at sites of colocalized Kv2.1 and RyR clusters as determined by post-hoc immunolabeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 confirm that the Ca2+ signals observed with GCaMP3-Kv2.1 also occur at endogenous Kv2.1 clusters using a different Ca2+ indicator. Post-hoc immunolabeling provides direct evidence for colocalization with Kv2.1 and RyRs. This addresses a potential concern that the GCaMP3-Kv2.1 construct itself might alter Ca2+ signaling.

results.result: Localized Ca2+ signals at Kv2.1 clusters are Ca2+ sparks mediated by LTCCs and RyRs. Caffeine enhances spark frequency, thapsigargin eliminates sparks, Bay K8644 increases spark frequency, and nimodipine rapidly inhibits sparks. Post-hoc immunolabeling confirms that GCaMP3-Kv2.1 clusters producing sparks colocalize with RyRs. Spark frequency but not amplitude correlates with RyR cluster size, and Bay K8644 steepens this relationship.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 provide strong pharmacological evidence that the localized Ca2+ signals are LTCC- and RyR-mediated Ca2+ sparks. The use of multiple pharmacological agents with known mechanisms (caffeine, thapsigargin, Bay K8644, nimodipine) provides converging evidence. Post-hoc immunolabeling (C71) directly links spark-producing clusters to RyRs. The correlation between spark frequency and RyR cluster size (C72, C73) is consistent with findings in other cell types (citations provided).

results.result: Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyR2 can spatially associate in HEK293T cells and generate spontaneous Ca2+ release events that are blocked by the RyR inhibitor tetracaine. Expressing Kv2.1 enhances spark frequency and amplitude. Clustering-competent Kv2.1 (WT and P404W) increases spark frequency, while non-clustering Kv2.1S586A does not. Spark amplitude is enhanced by K+-conducting Kv2.1WT but not Kv2.1P404W, suggesting clustering affects frequency while K+ conductance affects amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C82 demonstrate that the Kv2.1-LTCC-RyR triad can be reconstituted in a heterologous system and generate functional Ca2+ sparks. The use of tetracaine (C77) confirms RyR involvement. The differential effects of clustering-competent vs. non-clustering Kv2.1 mutants (C79, C80) and conducting vs. nonconducting mutants (C81) provide mechanistic insights. The interpretation that clustering affects frequency while conductance affects amplitude (C81) is reasonable but speculative regarding the mechanism in HEK293T cells.

results.result: Kv2.1 enhances Cav1.2 activity in HEK293T cells. Coexpression of Cav1.2 with Kv2.1P404W enhances peak ICa, shifts the voltage-dependence of activation to more negative voltages, and increases Ca2+-dependent inactivation (CDI). In the presence of STAC1, which reduces CDI, the increase in ICa and hyperpolarized activation shift persist but CDI is normalized. Kv2.1P404W enhances Cav1.2-mediated Ca2+ influx measured by Rhod-2 and Fluo-4 fluorescence. Gating current analysis shows that nitrendipine-sensitive Qon is comparable with or without Kv2.1, but Itail is significantly greater with Kv2.1, indicating enhanced voltage sensor coupling to channel opening.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C92 provide comprehensive electrophysiological evidence that Kv2.1 enhances LTCC activity through a mechanism involving enhanced voltage sensor coupling to channel opening. The use of the nonconducting Kv2.1P404W mutant isolates the effect from K+ conductance. Multiple approaches (whole-cell currents, G-V analysis, Ca2+ imaging, gating currents) provide converging evidence. The gating current analysis (C90, C91) is particularly strong, showing that the effect is not due to increased channel number but enhanced coupling efficiency. The STAC1 experiments (C86, C87) provide additional mechanistic insights into CDI.

results.result: Kv2.1 enhances spontaneous Cav1.2 channel openings at hyperpolarized membrane potentials in HEK293T cells. Cells coexpressing Cav1.2 and DsRed-Kv2.1P404W display significantly more Ca2+ sparklets than control cells at -70 mV holding potential, with higher basal activity (nPs). Bay K8644 treatment does not further enhance nPs in cells expressing Kv2.1P404W, suggesting near-maximal activation. The nearest-neighbor distance of sparklet sites is significantly reduced in the presence of Kv2.1.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 provide direct evidence for enhanced spontaneous LTCC openings at hyperpolarized potentials using Ca2+ sparklet imaging. The finding that Bay K8644 has no additional effect (C94) suggests that Kv2.1 produces near-maximal activation at this potential, which is a strong result. The reduced nearest-neighbor distance (C95) indicates that Kv2.1 increases the proximity of active channels, consistent with the clustering data. The sparklet approach provides single-channel resolution and complements the whole-cell electrophysiology.

results.result: Kv2.1 enhances endogenous LTCC activity in CHNs. Whole-cell Ba2+ currents and LTCC tail currents are larger in WT CHNs than in Kv2.1 KO CHNs. The reduced current in Kv2.1 KO CHNs is primarily due to reduction in the nimodipine-sensitive (LTCC) component. Nimodipine-sensitive Qon is not significantly different between WT and Kv2.1 KO CHNs, but peak Itail is reduced in Kv2.1 KO CHNs, suggesting enhanced coupling efficiency between LTCC voltage-sensor movement and channel opening in the presence of Kv2.1.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 extend the findings from heterologous expression to endogenous channels in neurons, demonstrating physiological relevance. The use of Kv2.1 KO CHNs provides a strong genetic control. The gating current analysis (C99, C100) parallels the findings in HEK293T cells and supports the same mechanism. The consistency between HEK293T and CHN results strengthens the overall conclusion.

results.result: Cav1.2 labeling is increased in pyramidal neurons in area CA1 in Kv2.1 KO brain sections, both within cell bodies and apical dendrites, potentially as a compensatory mechanism to overcome reduced Cav1.2 channel function.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 identify a compensatory upregulation of Cav1.2 expression in adult Kv2.1 KO mice. The interpretation as a compensatory mechanism (C103) is reasonable given the reduced LTCC function demonstrated in C97-C101, though it remains inferential. This finding highlights the importance of Kv2.1 for LTCC function in vivo.

results.result: Kv2.1 KO CHNs have reduced colocalization between Cav1.2 clusters and RyRs, decreased RyR cluster size, and increased distance between Cav1.2 clusters compared to WT CHNs. The number of Cav1.2 clusters per μm² does not differ between WT and Kv2.1 KO CHNs, suggesting that Kv2.1 promotes spatial coupling of Cav1.2 to RyRs without affecting Cav1.2 cluster number in cultured neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 demonstrate that loss of Kv2.1 impairs the spatial organization of Cav1.2 and RyRs in CHNs, consistent with the gain-of-function experiments in HEK293T cells. The finding that Cav1.2 cluster number is unchanged (C107) indicates the effect is on spatial organization rather than expression, contrasting with the in vivo upregulation (C102). This difference between cultured neurons and adult brain is appropriately noted.

results.result: Loss of Kv2.1 is associated with a significant reduction in Ca2+ spark frequency in CHNs. Spontaneous sparks in WT mouse CHNs are associated with Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyR clusters identified by post-hoc immunolabeling. These findings demonstrate that Kv2.1 channels promote the spatial and functional association of endogenous Cav1.2 and RyRs in neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 provide functional evidence that loss of Kv2.1 impairs Ca2+ spark generation, consistent with the reduced spatial coupling (C104-C106) and reduced LTCC currents (C97-C101). Post-hoc immunolabeling (C109) confirms the association of sparks with Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyR clusters in WT neurons. The conclusion (C111) is well-supported by the combined data from gain-of-function (HEK293T) and loss-of-function (Kv2.1 KO CHNs) experiments.

results.result: The authors propose a model in which Kv2.1 serves a nonconducting function to anchor the ER to the PM via interaction with VAP proteins and to promote organization of Cav1.2 channels into clusters in apposition to ER-localized RyRs. Kv2.1-mediated clustering increases Cav1.2 activity, enhancing spontaneous openings at negative potentials, allowing Ca2+ entry that activates nearby RyRs by CICR to generate Ca2+ sparks independently of action potentials.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 present the overall model integrating the findings. The model is well-supported by the data presented in the manuscript, including spatial association (C21-C40), clustering effects (C41-C55), enhanced LTCC activity (C83-C101), and Ca2+ spark generation (C67-C74, C109-C111). The nonconducting function is supported by experiments with Kv2.1P404W. The independence from action potentials is supported by C62-C64.

results.result: Colocalization of LTCCs with Kv2.1 is dynamically regulated by neuronal activity (glutamate and TTX treatments). LTCCs are recruited to Kv2.1-associated EPJs, a property not shared by T-type Ca2+ channels. The proteins mediating Cav1.2 clustering in dendritic spines and at somatic EPJs may be distinct. Kv2.1 clustering and EPJ induction is necessary for spatial association with LTCCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 summarize key mechanistic findings from the Discussion. C117 is supported by C29-C30. C118 is supported by C53. C119 is a reasonable inference from the proteomic data (C37-C38) showing absence of known spine LTCC clustering proteins. C120 is supported by the Kv2.1S586A experiments (C50).

results.result: The authors speculate that tethering of LTCCs at Kv2-associated EPJs could be mediated by an intermediary recruited to Kv2.1-mediated EPJs. It is unlikely that RyRs are directly recruited to EPJs by Kv2 channels, as RyR clusters persist in neurons lacking Kv2 channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C122 are speculative regarding the molecular mechanism. C121 is presented as speculation with appropriate caveats. C122 is supported by citations to prior work showing RyR persistence in Kv2 KO neurons, but the mechanism of RyR localization to EPJs remains unclear. These are reasonable interpretations but require further experimental validation.

results.result: LTCC activity is sensitive to spatial organization in the PM. Kv2.1 influences subcellular localization and activity of somatic Cav1.2 channels, increasing both clustering and opening at polarized Vm. The reduced LTCC currents and impaired Cav1.2-RyR association in Kv2.1 KO CHNs suggests Kv2.1 serves a dual targeting/modulation function. Kv2.1 increases whole-cell Cav1.2 current amplitude without changing the number of PM channels, suggesting enhanced coupling of voltage sensor movement to channel opening.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 summarize the key findings regarding LTCC regulation by Kv2.1. C123 is supported by citations to prior work. C124-C127 are well-supported by the electrophysiology data (C83-C101) and gating current analysis (C90-C92, C99-C100). The dual targeting/modulation function (C125) is a reasonable synthesis of the spatial and functional data.

results.result: The authors propose three possible mechanisms for Kv2.1-dependent increase in LTCC activity: (1) Kv2.1-induced clustering increases physical interactions between Cav1.2 channels promoting cooperative gating; (2) Kv2.1 functions as an auxiliary voltage sensor for Cav1.2 through direct intermolecular interaction; (3) Cav1.2 is modulated by signaling molecules encountered when recruited to EPJs by Kv2.1.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 present three speculative mechanisms. C128 is supported by analogy to optogenetic clustering studies (citations provided) but lacks direct evidence for cooperative gating. C129 is speculative and would require demonstration of direct interaction and functional coupling. C130 is plausible given the known presence of kinases at EPJs but lacks direct evidence. These are reasonable hypotheses for future investigation but remain unproven.

results.result: Ca2+ spark frequency is modulated by LTCC agonists and antagonists and is reduced by loss of Kv2.1 expression. Only a subset of Kv2.1-associated EPJs possess the molecular machinery to generate Ca2+ sparks. Kv2.1-mediated somatodendritic EPJs provide a platform for localized Ca2+ elevation at individual EPJs without increasing global Ca2+. Sparks can occur independently in neighboring Kv2.1-containing EPJs, suggesting compartmentalized Ca2+ signaling in aspiny neuronal regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 summarize the Ca2+ signaling findings. C131 is supported by C67-C70. C132 is supported by C110. C133 is a reasonable inference from C58, C71. C134 is supported by the observation of localized vs. global signals (C57-C59). C135 is supported by C59 and provides an important functional interpretation.

results.result: Somatic LTCC- and RyR-mediated Ca2+ release activates KCa3.1 channels in hippocampal neurons. Somatodendritic LTCCs are preferentially coupled to activation of signaling pathways resulting in gene expression changes. Kv2.1-mediated organization and regulation of somatic LTCCs provides a mechanism to control local Ca2+ influx and organize Ca2+ signaling microdomains.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C138 place the findings in broader context. C136 and C137 are supported by citations to prior work. C138 is a reasonable synthesis of the current findings and their implications. These claims appropriately connect the current work to established functions of somatic LTCCs.

results.result: Acute ischemic or depolarizing events lead to Ca2+-dependent dispersal of Kv2.1 clusters, potentially as a homeostatic mechanism. The Ca2+-dependent dispersal of Kv2.1 clusters and resulting dissociation of Cav1.2 and RyRs may represent a negative feedback loop to limit excessive Ca2+ increases. Activity-dependent declustering of Kv2.1 may reduce LTCC currents through increased Kv2.1 currents and altered Cav1.2 spatial organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 propose a homeostatic feedback mechanism. C139 is supported by citations to prior work. C140 and C141 are reasonable inferences from the current findings (C29-C30) combined with prior knowledge, though they remain speculative regarding the physiological function. The proposed mechanism is plausible and testable.

results.result: The spatial association of Kv2.1, Cav1.2, and RyRs is preserved in intact adult mouse and rat brains and can be recapitulated in heterologous cells. Somatodendritic Ca2+ sparks have been observed in acute hippocampal slices from rats aged P3-P80, suggesting functional roles that emerge early and continue beyond development.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C143 address the physiological relevance and developmental aspects. C142 is supported by the brain section data (C32-C36) and HEK293T reconstitution (C75-C82). C143 is supported by citation to prior work and suggests the findings are relevant across development. These claims appropriately contextualize the in vitro findings.
